arXiv:1202.6662v2 [math.AG] 31 May 2013

Okounkov bodies and Seshadri constants

Atsushi Ito Address: Graduate School of Mathematical Sciences, the University of Tokyo, 3-8-1 Komaba, Meguro-ku, Tokyo 153-8914, Japan. Email address: itoatsu@ms.u-tokyo.ac.jp
Abstract.

Okounkov bodies, which are closed convex sets defined for big line bundles, have rich information on the line bundles. On the other hand, Seshadri constants are invariants which measure the positivity of line bundles. In this paper, we prove that Okounkov bodies give lower bounds of Seshadri constants.

Key words and phrases: 
Okounkov body, Seshadri constant, graded linear series
2010 Mathematics Subject Classification
14C20;14M25

1. Introduction

In this paper, we investigate a relation between Okounkov bodies and Seshadri constants.

Okounkov bodies were introduced by Lazarsfeld and Mustaţă [LM] and independently by Kaveh and Khovanskii [KK], based on the work of Okounkov [Ok1, Ok2]. First, recall the definition of Okounkov bodies.

Let XX be a variety of dimension nn, z=(z1,…,zn)z=(z_{1},\ldots,z_{n}) a local coordinate system at a smooth point p∈Xp\in X, and >> a monomial order on ℕn\mathbb{N}^{n}. Then we obtain a valuation

ν=νz,>:𝒪X,p∖{0}→ℕn\nu=\nu_{z,>}:\mathcal{O}_{X,p}\setminus\{0\}\rightarrow\mathbb{N}^{n}

as follows; for f∈𝒪X,p∖{0}f\in\mathcal{O}_{X,p}\setminus\{0\}, we expand it as a formal power series

f=∑u∈ℕncu​zuf=\sum_{u\in\mathbb{N}^{n}}c_{u}z^{u}

and set

ν⁡(f):=min⁡{u|cu≠0},\nu(f):=\min\{\,u\,|\,c_{u}\not=0\},

where the minimum is taken with respect to the monomial order >>.

Let LL be a big line bundle on a projective variety XX. Then we can define the Okounkov body Δ⁡(L)\Delta(L) of LL as follows.

Fix an isomorphism Lp≅𝒪X,pL_{p}\cong\mathcal{O}_{X,p}. Then this isomorphism naturally induces Lpk≅𝒪X,pL^{k}_{p}\cong\mathcal{O}_{X,p} for any k≥0k\geq 0, and we have the map

H0​(X,k​L)∖{0}↪Lpk∖{0}≅𝒪X,p∖{0}→νℕn.H^{0}(X,kL)\setminus\{0\}\hookrightarrow L^{k}_{p}\setminus\{0\}\cong\mathcal{O}_{X,p}\setminus\{0\}\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\nu}}{{\to}}\mathbb{N}^{n}.

We write ν⁡(H0​(X,k​L))⊂ℕn\nu(H^{0}(X,kL))\subset\mathbb{N}^{n} for the image of H0​(X,k​L)∖{0}H^{0}(X,kL)\setminus\{0\} by this map. Note that ν​(H0​(X,k​L))\nu(H^{0}(X,kL)) does not depend on the choice of the isomorphism Lp≅𝒪X,pL_{p}\cong\mathcal{O}_{X,p} because ν\nu maps any unit element in 𝒪X,p\mathcal{O}_{X,p} to 0∈ℕn0\in\mathbb{N}^{n}. Then

ΓL=ΓL,z,>:=⋃k∈ℕ{k}×ν⁡(H0​(X,k​L))⊂ℕ×ℕn\Gamma_{L}=\Gamma_{L,z,>}:=\bigcup_{k\in\mathbb{N}}\{k\}\times\nu(H^{0}(X,kL))\subset\mathbb{N}\times\mathbb{N}^{n}

is a semigroup by construction. We define the Okounkov body of LL with respect to zz and >> by

Δ⁡(L)=Δz,>​(L):\displaystyle\Delta(L)=\Delta_{z,>}(L): =closed convex hull​(⋃k≥11k​ν​(H0​(X,k​L)))\displaystyle=\text{closed convex hull}\,\Big(\bigcup_{k\geq 1}\frac{1}{k}\nu(H^{0}(X,kL))\Big)
=Σ⁡(ΓL)∩({1}×ℝn),\displaystyle=\Sigma(\Gamma_{L})\cap(\{1\}\times\mathbb{R}^{n}),

where Σ⁡(ΓL)\Sigma(\Gamma_{L}) is the closed convex cone spanned by ΓL\Gamma_{L}.

More generally, we can define the Okounkov body for a graded linear series. That is, for a graded linear series W∙W_{\bullet} associated to a line bundle LL on a (not necessarily projective) variety XX, we set

ΓW∙=ΓW∙,z,>:=⋃k∈ℕ{k}×ν⁡(Wk)⊂ℕ×ℕn.\Gamma_{W_{\bullet}}=\Gamma_{W_{\bullet},z,>}:=\bigcup_{k\in\mathbb{N}}\{k\}\times\nu(W_{k})\subset\mathbb{N}\times\mathbb{N}^{n}.

We define the Okounkov body of W∙W_{\bullet} with respect to zz and >> by Δ⁡(W∙)=Δz,>​(W∙):=Σ⁡(ΓW∙,z,>)∩({1}×ℝn)\Delta(W_{\bullet})=\Delta_{z,>}(W_{\bullet}):=\Sigma(\Gamma_{W_{\bullet},z,>})\cap(\{1\}\times\mathbb{R}^{n}).

Remark 1.1.

In [LM], they use “admissible flags” instead of local coordinate systems. Essentially, there is no difference if >> is the lexicographic order. Local coordinate systems are used in [BC] for instance.

On the other hand, Demailly [De] defined an interesting invariant, Seshadri constant, which measures the local positivity of an ample line bundle at a point. Seshadri constants relate to jet separation of adjoint bundles, Ross-Thomas’ slope stabilities of polarized varieties [RT], Gromov width (an invariant in symplectic geometry) [MP], and so on. Nakamaye [Na] defined Seshadri constants at very general points for big line bundles. For a detailed treatment of Seshadri constants, we refer the reader to [La, Chapter 5] or [B+].

We extend the notion of Seshadri constants slightly. Usually, Seshadri constants are defined in a numerical way. However, we adopt an equivalent definition in terms of jet separation since we treat graded linear series in this paper.

Let W∙W_{\bullet} be a “birational” graded linear series associated to a line bundle LL on a variety XX (see Definition 3.2 for the definition of a birational graded linear series). Using jet separation (cf. [De, Theorem 6.4], [ELMNP, Proposition 6.6]), we define the Seshadri constant ε⁡(W∙,1)\varepsilon(W_{\bullet};1) of W∙W_{\bullet} at a very general point by

ε⁡(W∙,1):=supk>0s⁡(Wk,1)k∈ℝ+∪{+∞},\varepsilon(W_{\bullet};1):=\sup_{k>0}\frac{s(W_{k};1)}{k}\in{\mathbb{R}}_{+}\cup\{+\infty\},

where s⁡(Wk,1)s(W_{k};1) is the supremum of integers s≥−1s\geq-1 such that the natural map Wk↪H0​(X,Lk)→Lk⊗𝒪X/𝔪ps+1W_{k}\hookrightarrow H^{0}(X,L^{k})\rightarrow L^{k}\otimes\mathcal{O}_{X}/\mathfrak{m}_{p}^{s+1} is surjective for a very general point p∈Xp\in X. When LL is a big line bundle on a projective variety XX and W∙={H0​(X,k​L)}kW_{\bullet}=\{H^{0}(X,kL)\}_{k}, it is easy to show W∙W_{\bullet} is birational. Hence we can consider the Seshadri constant of W∙W_{\bullet} at a very general point, which we denote by ε⁡(L,1)\varepsilon(L;1) or ε⁡(X,L,1)\varepsilon(X,L;1).

To relate Seshadri constants with Okounkov bodies, we introduce an invariant for a convex set. For an integral polytope Δ⊂ℝn\Delta\subset\mathbb{R}^{n} of dimension nn, we can consider an invariant ε⁡(Δ,1):=ε⁡(XΔ,LΔ,1)\varepsilon(\Delta;1):=\varepsilon(X_{\Delta},L_{\Delta};1), where (XΔ,LΔ)(X_{\Delta},L_{\Delta}) is the polarized toric variety corresponding to Δ\Delta. To generalize this invariant to an nn-dimensional convex set Δ\Delta, we introduce a “monomial” birational graded linear series WΔ,∙W_{\Delta,\bullet} associated to 𝒪(ℂ×)n\mathcal{O}_{(\mathbb{C}^{\times})^{n}} on (ℂ×)n(\mathbb{C}^{\times})^{n} (see Definition 4.1). Thus we can define ε⁡(Δ,1):=ε⁡((ℂ×)n,WΔ,∙,1)\varepsilon(\Delta;1):=\varepsilon((\mathbb{C}^{\times})^{n},W_{\Delta,\bullet};1).

In this paper, we show the following theorem, which states that Okounkov bodies give lower bounds on Seshadri constants.

Theorem 1.2 (Special case of Theorem 5.8).

Let XX be a projective variety of dimension nn, and fix a local coordinate system z=(z1,…,zn)z=(z_{1},\ldots,z_{n}) on XX at a smooth point and a monomial order >> on ℕn\mathbb{N}^{n}. For a big line bundle LL on XX, it holds that ε⁡(L,1)≥ε⁡(Δz,>​(L),1)\varepsilon(L;1)\geq\varepsilon(\Delta_{z,>}(L);1).

We explain the idea of the proof of Theorem 1.2 when LL is ample. The strategy is to compare two graded linear series {H0​(X,k​L)}k\{H^{0}(X,kL)\}_{k} and W​(ΓL)∙:={⨁u∈ν⁡(H0​(X,k​L))ℂ​xu}kW(\Gamma_{L})_{\bullet}:=\{\bigoplus_{u\in\nu(H^{0}(X,kL))}\mathbb{C}x^{u}\}_{k}. Note that ⨁u∈ν⁡(H0​(X,k​L))ℂ​xu⊂ℂ⁡[ℕn]\bigoplus_{u\in\nu(H^{0}(X,kL))}\mathbb{C}x^{u}\subset\mathbb{C}[\mathbb{N}^{n}] is nothing but the degree kk-th part of the graded ring ℂ⁡[ΓL]\mathbb{C}[\Gamma_{L}].

If ΓL\Gamma_{L} is finitely generated, Anderson [An] showed that ⨁kH0​(X,k​L)\bigoplus_{k}H^{0}(X,kL) degenerates to ℂ⁡[ΓL]\mathbb{C}[\Gamma_{L}]. In other words, (X,L)(X,L) degenerates to the (not necessarily normal) toric variety (Proj⁡ℂ⁡[ΓL],𝒪⁡(1))(\Proj\mathbb{C}[\Gamma_{L}],\mathcal{O}(1)). Since Seshadri constants have a lower semicontinuity, we have ε⁡(X,L,1)≥ε⁡(Proj⁡ℂ⁡[ΓL],𝒪⁡(1),1)\varepsilon(X,L;1)\geq\varepsilon(\Proj\mathbb{C}[\Gamma_{L}],\mathcal{O}(1);1). It is easy to check that ε⁡(Proj⁡ℂ⁡[ΓL],𝒪⁡(1),1)=ε⁡(XΔ⁡(L),LΔ⁡(L),1)=ε⁡(Δ⁡(L),1)\varepsilon(\Proj\mathbb{C}[\Gamma_{L}],\mathcal{O}(1);1)=\varepsilon(X_{\Delta(L)},L_{\Delta(L)};1)=\varepsilon(\Delta(L);1), and Theorem 1.2 follows in this case.

Unfortunately, ΓL\Gamma_{L} is not finitely generated in general. Hence we cannot use the degeneration of the section ring ⨁kH0​(X,k​L)\bigoplus_{k}H^{0}(X,kL). Instead, we degenerate linear series as in [CM], that is, we degenerate H0​(X,k​L)H^{0}(X,kL) to W​(ΓL)k=⨁u∈ν⁡(H0​(X,k​L))ℂ​xuW(\Gamma_{L})_{k}=\bigoplus_{u\in\nu(H^{0}(X,kL))}\mathbb{C}x^{u} for each kk separately. Then we can show s⁡(H0​(X,k​L),1)≥s⁡(W​(ΓL)k,1)s(H^{0}(X,kL);1)\geq s(W(\Gamma_{L})_{k};1) and compare the Seshadri constants of LL and W​(ΓL)∙W(\Gamma_{L})_{\bullet}.

Thus even if we show Theorem 1.2 only for an ample line bundle LL, we have to treat the graded linear series W​(ΓL)∙W(\Gamma_{L})_{\bullet}. This is the reason why we extend the notion of Seshadri constants to graded linear series.

The definition of Seshadri constants can be easily generalized to the multi-point case (cf. [La],[B+]). That is, we can define the Seshadri constants ε⁡(W∙,𝐦)\varepsilon(W_{\bullet};\mathbf{m}) and ε⁡(Δ,𝐦)\varepsilon(\Delta;\mathbf{m}) for a weight 𝐦=(m1,…,mr)∈ℝ+r\mathbf{m}=(m_{1},\ldots,m_{r})\in{\mathbb{R}}_{+}^{r}.

Theorem 1.2 is generalized to the multi-point case and birational graded linear series as follows.

Theorem 1.3 (=Theorem 5.8).

Let W∙W_{\bullet} be a birational graded linear series associated to a line bundle LL on an nn-dimensional variety XX. Fix a local coordinate system z=(z1,…,zn)z=(z_{1},\ldots,z_{n}) on XX at a smooth point and a monomial order >> on ℕn\mathbb{N}^{n}. Then ε⁡(W∙,𝐦)≥ε⁡(Δz,>​(W∙),𝐦)\varepsilon(W_{\bullet};\mathbf{m})\geq\varepsilon(\Delta_{z,>}(W_{\bullet});\mathbf{m}) holds for any r∈ℤ+r\in{\mathbb{Z}}_{+} and 𝐦∈ℝ+r\mathbf{m}\in{\mathbb{R}}_{+}^{r}.

This paper is organized as follows. In Section 2, we recall some notations and conventions. In Section 3, we define Seshadri constants of graded linear series and investigate basic properties. In Section 4, we study Seshadri constants of monomial graded linear series. In Section 5, we give the proof of Theorem 1.3. Throughout this paper, we consider varieties or schemes over the complex number field ℂ\mathbb{C}.

2. Notations and conventions

We denote by ℕ,ℤ,ℚ,ℝ\mathbb{N},\mathbb{Z},\mathbb{Q},\mathbb{R}, and ℂ\mathbb{C} the set of all natural numbers, integers, rational numbers, real numbers, and complex numbers respectively. In this paper, ℕ\mathbb{N} contains 00. Set ℤ+=ℕ∖0{\mathbb{Z}}_{+}=\mathbb{N}\setminus 0, ℝ+={x∈ℝ|x>0}{\mathbb{R}}_{+}=\{x\in\mathbb{R}\,|\,x>0\}. For a real number t∈ℝt\in\mathbb{R}, the round up of tt is denoted by ⌈t⌉∈ℤ\lceil t\rceil\in\mathbb{Z}.

For a subset S⊂ℝnS\subset\mathbb{R}^{n}, we denote by Σ⁡(S)\Sigma(S) the closed convex cone spanned by SS. For t∈ℝt\in\mathbb{R}, we set t​S={t​u|u∈S}tS=\{\,tu\,|\,u\in S\}. For another subset S′⊂ℝnS^{\prime}\subset\mathbb{R}^{n}, S+S′={u+u′|u∈S,u′∈S′}S+S^{\prime}=\{u+u^{\prime}\,|\,u\in S,u^{\prime}\in S^{\prime}\} is the Minkowski sum of SS and S′S^{\prime}. For simplicity of notation, we denote S+(−S′)S+(-S^{\prime}) by S−S′S-S^{\prime}. For u′∈ℝnu^{\prime}\in\mathbb{R}^{n}, S+u′={u+u′|u∈S}S+u^{\prime}=\{u+u^{\prime}\,|\,u\in S\} is the parallel translation of SS by u′u^{\prime}.

For a convex set Δ⊂ℝn\Delta\subset\mathbb{R}^{n}, the dimension of Δ\Delta is the dimension of the affine space spanned by Δ\Delta. We denote by Δ∘\Delta^{\circ} the interior of Δ\Delta.

A subset P⊂ℝnP\subset\mathbb{R}^{n} is called a polytope if it is the convex hull of a finite set in ℝn\mathbb{R}^{n}. A polytope PP is integral if all its vertices are contained in ℤn\mathbb{Z}^{n}.

For a variety XX, we say a property holds at a general point of XX if it holds for all points in the complement of a proper algebraic subset. A property holds at a very general point of XX if it holds for all points in the complement of the union of countably many proper subvarieties.

Throughout this paper, a divisor means a Cartier divisor. Thus we use the words “divisor”, “line bundle”, and “invertible sheaf ” interchangeably. For divisors DD and D′D^{\prime}, the inequality D≥D′D\geq D^{\prime} means D−D′D-D^{\prime} is effective.

3. Seshadri constants of graded linear series

In this section, we define Seshadri constants of graded linear series.

Definition 3.1.

Let LL be a line bundle on a (not necessarily projective) variety XX, and WW a subspace of H0​(X,L)H^{0}(X,L). For r∈ℤ+r\in{\mathbb{Z}}_{+} and 𝐦=(m1,…,mr)∈ℤr\mathbf{m}=(m_{1},\ldots,m_{r})\in\mathbb{Z}^{r}, we say that WW separates 𝐦\mathbf{m}-jets at smooth rr points p1,…,prp_{1},\ldots,p_{r} in XX if the natural map

W→L/(L⊗⨂i=1r𝔪pimi+1)=⨁i=1rL/𝔪pimi+1​L\ W\rightarrow L\big/\Big(L\otimes\bigotimes_{i=1}^{r}\mathfrak{m}_{p_{i}}^{m_{i}+1}\Big)=\bigoplus_{i=1}^{r}L/\mathfrak{m}_{p_{i}}^{m_{i}+1}L

is surjective, where we regard 𝔪pimi+1=𝒪X\mathfrak{m}_{p_{i}}^{m_{i}+1}=\mathcal{O}_{X} for mi≤−1m_{i}\leq-1. We say WW generically separates 𝐦\mathbf{m}-jets if WW separates 𝐦\mathbf{m}-jets at general rr points in XX. By definition, any WW generically separates 𝐦\mathbf{m}-jets if mi≤−1m_{i}\leq-1 for any ii.

For W⊂H0​(X,L)W\subset H^{0}(X,L) and 𝐦=(m1,…,mr)∈ℝ+r\mathbf{m}=(m_{1},\ldots,m_{r})\in{\mathbb{R}}_{+}^{r}, we define s⁡(W,𝐦)∈ℝ∪{+∞}s(W;\mathbf{m})\in\mathbb{R}\cup\{+\infty\} to be

s⁡(W,𝐦)=sup{t∈ℝ|W​generically separates ⌈t​𝐦⌉-jets},s(W;\mathbf{m})=\sup\{\,t\in\mathbb{R}\,|\,W\ \text{generically separates $\lceil t\mathbf{m}\rceil$-jets}\},

where ⌈t​𝐦⌉=(⌈t​m1⌉,…,⌈t​mr⌉)\lceil t\mathbf{m}\rceil=(\lceil tm_{1}\rceil,\ldots,\lceil tm_{r}\rceil). When dimW<+∞\dim W<+\infty, we have

s⁡(W,𝐦)=max⁡{t∈ℝ|W​generically separates ⌈t​𝐦⌉-jets}∈ℝ.s(W;\mathbf{m})=\max\{\,t\in\mathbb{R}\,|\,W\ \text{generically separates $\lceil t\mathbf{m}\rceil$-jets}\}\in\mathbb{R}.

When W=H0​(X,L)W=H^{0}(X,L), we denote s⁡(W,𝐦)s(W,\mathbf{m}) by s⁡(L,𝐦)s(L;\mathbf{m}).

Suppose XX is a variety of dimension nn and LL is a line bundle on XX. Let W∙={Wk}k∈ℕW_{\bullet}=\{W_{k}\}_{k\in\mathbb{N}} be a graded linear series associated to LL, i.e., WkW_{k} is a subspace of H0​(X,k​L)H^{0}(X,kL) for any k≥0k\geq 0 with W0=ℂW_{0}=\mathbb{C}, such that ⨁k≥0Wk\bigoplus_{k\geq 0}W_{k} is a graded subalgebra of the section ring ⨁k≥0H0​(X,k​L)\bigoplus_{k\geq 0}H^{0}(X,kL). When all WkW_{k} are finite dimensional, W∙W_{\bullet} is called of finite dimensional type.

Definition 3.2.

A graded linear series W∙W_{\bullet} on a variety XX is birational if the function field K⁡(X)K(X) of XX is generated by {f/g∈K(X)|f,g∈Wk,g≠0}\{\,f/g\in K(X)\,|\,f,g\in W_{k},g\not=0\} over ℂ\mathbb{C} for any k≫0k\gg 0. When W∙W_{\bullet} is of finite dimensional type, this is clearly equivalent to the condition that the rational map defined by |Wk||W_{k}| is birational onto its image for any k≫0k\gg 0, which is Condition (B) in [LM, Definition 2.5].

Now we define Seshadri constants of graded linear series.

Definition 3.3.

Let W∙W_{\bullet} be a birational graded linear series associated to a line bundle LL on a variety XX. For 𝐦=(m1,…,mr)∈ℝ+r\mathbf{m}=(m_{1},\ldots,m_{r})\in{\mathbb{R}}_{+}^{r}, we define the Seshadri constant of W∙W_{\bullet} at very general points with weight 𝐦\mathbf{m} to be

ε⁡(X,W∙,𝐦)=ε⁡(W∙,𝐦):=supk>0s⁡(Wk,𝐦)k∈ℝ+∪{+∞}.\varepsilon(X,W_{\bullet};\mathbf{m})=\varepsilon(W_{\bullet};\mathbf{m}):=\sup_{k>0}\dfrac{s(W_{k};\mathbf{m})}{k}\in{\mathbb{R}}_{+}\cup\{+\infty\}.

Note that s⁡(Wk,𝐦)>0s(W_{k};\mathbf{m})>0 holds for k≫0k\gg 0 by the birationality of W∙W_{\bullet}.

When Wk=H0​(X,k​L)W_{k}=H^{0}(X,kL) for any kk, we denote it by ε⁡(X,L,𝐦)\varepsilon(X,L;\mathbf{m}) or ε⁡(L,𝐦)\varepsilon(L;\mathbf{m}).

Remark 3.4.

The definition of Seshadri constants by jet separation is due to Theorem 6.4 in [De]. See also [La] or [ELMNP]. We treat the definition by blowing ups in Lemmas 3.9 and 3.10.

Remark 3.5.

By definition, s⁡(W,𝐦)≤s⁡(W′,𝐦)s(W;\mathbf{m})\leq s(W^{\prime};\mathbf{m}) holds for subspaces W⊂W′W\subset W^{\prime} in H0​(X,L)H^{0}(X,L). Thus ε(W∙;𝐦)≤ε(W∙′;𝐦)\varepsilon(W_{\bullet};\mathbf{m})\leq\varepsilon(W_{\bullet}^{{}^{\prime}};\mathbf{m}) holds for W∙,W∙′W_{\bullet},W_{\bullet}^{{}^{\prime}} associated to LL if Wk⊂Wk′W_{k}\subset W_{k}^{{}^{\prime}} for any kk (we write W∙⊂W∙′W_{\bullet}\subset W_{\bullet}^{{}^{\prime}} for such W∙,W∙′W_{\bullet},W_{\bullet}^{{}^{\prime}}).

For an injection L↪L′L\hookrightarrow L^{\prime} between line bundles on XX and a subspace W⊂H0​(X,L)W\subset H^{0}(X,L), s⁡(W,𝐦)s(W;\mathbf{m}) does not change if we regard WW as a subspace of H0​(X,L′)H^{0}(X,L^{\prime}) because we consider jet separation at general points. Hence ε⁡(W∙,𝐦)\varepsilon(W_{\bullet};\mathbf{m}) does not change for W∙W_{\bullet} associated to LL if we consider that W∙W_{\bullet} is associated to L′L^{\prime}.

Let π:X′→X\pi:X^{\prime}\rightarrow X be a birational morphism and W∙W_{\bullet} a graded linear series associated to LL on XX. Then we can consider that W∙W_{\bullet} is a graded linear series on X′X^{\prime} associated to π∗​L\pi^{*}L by the natural inclusion H0​(X,k​L)⊂H0​(X′,k​π∗​L)H^{0}(X,kL)\subset H^{0}(X^{\prime},k\pi^{*}L). By a similar reason to above, we have ε⁡(X,W∙,𝐦)=ε⁡(X′,W∙,𝐦)\varepsilon(X,W_{\bullet};\mathbf{m})=\varepsilon(X^{\prime},W_{\bullet};\mathbf{m}).

By the following lemma, we may assume that W∙W_{\bullet} is of finite dimensional type in many cases when we prove properties of ε⁡(X,W∙,𝐦)\varepsilon(X,W_{\bullet};\mathbf{m}).

Lemma 3.6.

Let W∙W_{\bullet} be a birational graded linear series. Suppose that W1,∙⊂W2,∙⊂⋯⊂Wl,∙⊂⋯⊂W∙W_{1,\bullet}\subset W_{2,\bullet}\subset\cdots\subset W_{l,\bullet}\subset\cdots\subset W_{\bullet} is an increasing sequence of birational graded linear series in W∙W_{\bullet} such that Wk=⋃l=1∞Wl,kW_{k}=\bigcup_{l=1}^{\infty}W_{l,k} for each kk. Then it holds that ε⁡(W∙,𝐦)=suplε⁡(Wl,∙,𝐦)=limlε⁡(Wl,∙,𝐦)\varepsilon(W_{\bullet};\mathbf{m})=\sup_{l}\varepsilon(W_{l,\bullet};\mathbf{m})=\lim_{l}\varepsilon(W_{l,\bullet};\mathbf{m}).

Proof.

Since ε⁡(Wl,∙,𝐦)\varepsilon(W_{l,\bullet};\mathbf{m}) is monotonically increasing, limlε⁡(Wl,∙,𝐦)\lim_{l}\varepsilon(W_{l,\bullet};\mathbf{m}) exists. The inequalities ε⁡(W∙,𝐦)≥suplε⁡(Wl,∙,𝐦)≥limlε⁡(Wl,∙,𝐦)\varepsilon(W_{\bullet};\mathbf{m})\geq\sup_{l}\varepsilon(W_{l,\bullet};\mathbf{m})\geq\lim_{l}\varepsilon(W_{l,\bullet};\mathbf{m}) are clear. Thus it is enough to show ε⁡(W∙,𝐦)≤limlε⁡(Wl,∙,𝐦)\varepsilon(W_{\bullet};\mathbf{m})\leq\lim_{l}\varepsilon(W_{l,\bullet};\mathbf{m}).

Fix kk and a real number t<s⁡(Wk,𝐦)t<s(W_{k};\mathbf{m}). By definition, WkW_{k} generically separates ⌈t​𝐦⌉\lceil t\mathbf{m}\rceil-jets. Hence Wl,kW_{l,k} also generically separates ⌈t​𝐦⌉\lceil t\mathbf{m}\rceil-jets for l≫0l\gg 0 by the assumption Wk=⋃lWl,kW_{k}=\bigcup_{l}W_{l,k}. Thus it holds that s⁡(Wk,𝐦)/k=limls⁡(Wl,k,𝐦)/k≤limlε⁡(Wl,∙,𝐦)s(W_{k};\mathbf{m})/k=\lim_{l}s(W_{l,k};\mathbf{m})/k\leq\lim_{l}\varepsilon(W_{l,\bullet};\mathbf{m}). By the definition of ε⁡(W∙,𝐦)\varepsilon(W_{\bullet};\mathbf{m}), we have ε⁡(W∙,𝐦)≤limlε⁡(Wl,∙,𝐦)\varepsilon(W_{\bullet};\mathbf{m})\leq\lim_{l}\varepsilon(W_{l,\bullet};\mathbf{m}). ∎

In Definition 3.3, ε⁡(W∙,𝐦)\varepsilon(W_{\bullet};\mathbf{m}) is defined by the supremum, but in fact it is the limit.

Lemma 3.7.

In Definition 3.3, ε⁡(W∙,𝐦)=lims⁡(Wk,𝐦)k\varepsilon(W_{\bullet};\mathbf{m})=\lim\dfrac{s(W_{k};\mathbf{m})}{k} holds.

Proof.

By Lemma 3.6, we may assume that W∙W_{\bullet} is of finite dimensional type. To prove this lemma, it suffices to show that a sequence {s⁡(Wk,𝐦)}k\{s(W_{k};\mathbf{m})\}_{k} is superadditive, i.e.,

s⁡(Wk+l,𝐦)≥s⁡(Wk,𝐦)+s⁡(Wl,𝐦)s(W_{k+l};\mathbf{m})\geq s(W_{k};\mathbf{m})+s(W_{l};\mathbf{m})

holds for k,l>0k,l>0 if s⁡(Wk,𝐦),s⁡(Wl,𝐦)≥0s(W_{k};\mathbf{m}),s(W_{l};\mathbf{m})\geq 0.

For simplicity, we set sk=s⁡(Wk,𝐦)s_{k}=s(W_{k};\mathbf{m}) in this proof. We prove the superadditivity only when r=1r=1, and write m∈ℝ+m\in{\mathbb{R}}_{+} instead of 𝐦\mathbf{m}. When r>1r>1, the proof is essentially the same. Hence we leave the details to the reader.

Fix a very general point p∈Xp\in X. For each k,i≥0k,i\geq 0, set

Wk,i=Wk∩H0​(X,Lk⊗𝔪pi)⊂H0​(X,Lk).W_{k,i}=W_{k}\cap H^{0}(X,L^{k}\otimes\mathfrak{m}_{p}^{i})\subset H^{0}(X,L^{k}).

For any s∈ℕs\in\mathbb{N}, it is easy to show that

Wk→Lk⊗𝒪X/𝔪ps+1W_{k}\rightarrow L^{k}\otimes\mathcal{O}_{X}/\mathfrak{m}_{p}^{s+1}

is surjective if and only if so is

Wk,i→Lk⊗𝔪pi/𝔪pi+1W_{k,i}\rightarrow L^{k}\otimes\mathfrak{m}_{p}^{i}/\mathfrak{m}_{p}^{i+1}

for each i∈{0,1,…,s}i\in\{0,1,\ldots,s\}.

Fix an integer 0≤i≤⌈sk​m⌉+⌈sl​m⌉0\leq i\leq\lceil s_{k}m\rceil+\lceil s_{l}m\rceil. Then there exist integers 0≤i1≤⌈sk​m⌉,0≤i2≤⌈sl​m⌉0\leq i_{1}\leq\lceil s_{k}m\rceil,0\leq i_{2}\leq\lceil s_{l}m\rceil such that i=i1+i2i=i_{1}+i_{2}. Consider the following diagram

In this diagram, α\alpha is surjective because i1≤⌈sk​m⌉,i2≤⌈sl​m⌉i_{1}\leq\lceil s_{k}m\rceil,i_{2}\leq\lceil s_{l}m\rceil, and β\beta is clearly surjective. Hence γ\gamma is also surjective for any i∈{0,1,…,⌈sk​m⌉+⌈sl​m⌉}i\in\{0,1,\ldots,\lceil s_{k}m\rceil+\lceil s_{l}m\rceil\}. Thus Wk+lW_{k+l} generically separates ⌈sk​m⌉+⌈sl​m⌉\lceil s_{k}m\rceil+\lceil s_{l}m\rceil-jets, which means

sk+l≥(⌈sk​m⌉+⌈sl​m⌉)/m≥sk+sl.∎s_{k+l}\geq(\lceil s_{k}m\rceil+\lceil s_{l}m\rceil)/m\geq s_{k}+s_{l}.\qed

Many properties of Seshadri constants of ample line bundles also hold for graded linear series.

Lemma 3.8.

For a birational graded linear series W∙W_{\bullet} (resp. W∙′W_{\bullet}^{{}^{\prime}}) associated to a line bundles LL (resp. L′L^{\prime}) on a variety XX and 𝐦∈ℝ+r\mathbf{m}\in{\mathbb{R}}_{+}^{r}, it holds that

  • (1)

    ε⁡(W∙(l),𝐦)=l⋅ε⁡(W∙,𝐦)\varepsilon(W_{\bullet}^{(l)};\mathbf{m})=l\cdot\varepsilon(W_{\bullet};\mathbf{m}) for l∈ℤ+l\in{\mathbb{Z}}_{+}, where W∙(l)W_{\bullet}^{(l)} is the graded linear series associated to LlL^{l} defined by Wk(l):=Wk​lW_{k}^{(l)}:=W_{kl}.

  • (2)

    ε⁡(W∙,t​𝐦)=t−1​ε​(W∙,𝐦)\varepsilon(W_{\bullet};t\mathbf{m})=t^{-1}\varepsilon(W_{\bullet};\mathbf{m}) for t∈ℝ+t\in{\mathbb{R}}_{+}.

  • (3)

    ε(W∙′′;𝐦)≥ε(W∙;𝐦)+ε(W∙′;𝐦)\varepsilon(W_{\bullet}^{{}^{\prime\prime}};\mathbf{m})\geq\varepsilon(W_{\bullet};\mathbf{m})+\varepsilon(W_{\bullet}^{{}^{\prime}};\mathbf{m}), where W∙′′W_{\bullet}^{{}^{\prime\prime}} is the graded linear series associated to L⊗L′L\otimes L^{\prime} defined by Wk′′:=the image of 
    Wk⊗Wk′→H0(X,k(L⊗L′))    W_{k}^{{}^{\prime\prime}}:=\text{the image of }\\ W_{k}\otimes W_{k}^{{}^{\prime}}\rightarrow H^{0}(X,k(L\otimes L^{\prime}))    .

  • (4)

    ε⁡(W∙,𝐦)≤vol⁡(W∙)/|𝐦|nn\varepsilon(W_{\bullet};\mathbf{m})\leq\sqrt[n]{{\vol(W_{\bullet})}/|\mathbf{m}|_{n}}, where n=dimXn=\dim X, vol⁡(W∙)=limkdimWkkn/n!\vol(W_{\bullet})=\lim_{k}\dfrac{\dim W_{k}}{k^{n}/n!}, and |𝐦|n=∑i=1rmin|\mathbf{m}|_{n}=\sum_{i=1}^{r}m_{i}^{n}.

Proof.

By Lemma 3.7, we have

ε⁡(W∙(l),𝐦)\displaystyle\varepsilon(W_{\bullet}^{(l)};\mathbf{m}) =limks⁡(Wk(l),𝐦)k\displaystyle=\lim_{k}\dfrac{s(W_{k}^{(l)};\mathbf{m})}{k}
=limks⁡(Wk​l,𝐦)k\displaystyle=\lim_{k}\dfrac{s(W_{kl};\mathbf{m})}{k}
=l⋅limks⁡(Wk​l,𝐦)k​l\displaystyle=l\cdot\lim_{k}\dfrac{s(W_{kl};\mathbf{m})}{kl}
=l⋅limks⁡(Wk,𝐦)k=l⋅ε⁡(W∙,𝐦).\displaystyle=l\cdot\lim_{k}\dfrac{s(W_{k};\mathbf{m})}{k}=l\cdot\varepsilon(W_{\bullet};\mathbf{m}).

Hence (1) is shown.

We can show (2) easily from the definition and the following.

s⁡(Wk,t​𝐦)\displaystyle s(W_{k};t\mathbf{m}) =sup{s∈ℝ|Wk​generically separates ⌈s​t​𝐦⌉-jets}\displaystyle=\sup\{\,s\in\mathbb{R}\,|\,W_{k}\ \text{generically separates $\lceil st\mathbf{m}\rceil$-jets}\,\}
=t−1​sup{s∈ℝ|Wk​generically separates ⌈s​𝐦⌉-jets}\displaystyle=t^{-1}\sup\{\,s\in\mathbb{R}\,|\,W_{k}\ \text{generically separates $\lceil s\mathbf{m}\rceil$-jets}\,\}
=t−1​s​(Wk,𝐦).\displaystyle=t^{-1}s(W_{k};\mathbf{m}).

To prove (3), it suffices to show s(Wk′′;𝐦)≥s(Wk;𝐦)+s(Wk′;𝐦)s(W_{k}^{{}^{\prime\prime}};\mathbf{m})\geq s(W_{k};\mathbf{m})+s(W_{k}^{{}^{\prime}};\mathbf{m}) for any kk. We can show this by the argument similar to the proof of Lemma 3.7. We leave the details to the reader.

To show (4), we fix a positive number 0<t<ε⁡(W∙,𝐦)0<t<\varepsilon(W_{\bullet};\mathbf{m}). By Lemma 3.7, the inequality s⁡(Wk,𝐦)>k​ts(W_{k};\mathbf{m})>kt holds for any k≫0k\gg 0. Thus WkW_{k} separates ⌈k​t​𝐦⌉\lceil kt\mathbf{m}\rceil-jets for any k≫0k\gg 0. In other words,

Wk→⨁iL⊗𝒪/𝔪pi⌈k​t​mi⌉+1W_{k}\rightarrow\bigoplus_{i}L\otimes\mathcal{O}/\mathfrak{m}_{p_{i}}^{\lceil ktm_{i}\rceil+1}

is surjective for very general p1,…,prp_{1},\ldots,p_{r}. This surjection induces

dimWk\displaystyle\dim W_{k} ≥dim⨁iL⊗𝒪/𝔪pi⌈k​t​mi⌉+1\displaystyle\geq\dim\bigoplus_{i}L\otimes\mathcal{O}/\mathfrak{m}_{p_{i}}^{\lceil ktm_{i}\rceil+1}
=∑i(⌈k​t​mi⌉+nn)=∑itn​minn!​kn+O⁡(kn−1).\displaystyle=\sum_{i}{\lceil ktm_{i}\rceil+n\choose n}=\sum_{i}\dfrac{t^{n}m_{i}^{n}}{n!}k^{n}+O(k^{n-1}).

Thus we have vol⁡(W∙)≥tn​|𝐦|n\vol(W_{\bullet})\geq t^{n}|\mathbf{m}|_{n} by k→+∞k\rightarrow+\infty. We finish the proof by t→ε⁡(W∙,𝐦)t\rightarrow\varepsilon(W_{\bullet};\mathbf{m}). ∎

Definition 3.3 is a natural generalization of the well-known definition of the Seshadri constant (at very general points) for a nef and big line bundle (cf. [La, Theorem 5.1.17]).

Lemma 3.9.

For a nef and big line bundle LL on a projective variety XX and 𝐦=(m1,…,mr)∈ℝ+r\mathbf{m}=(m_{1},\ldots,m_{r})\in{\mathbb{R}}_{+}^{r}, it holds that

ε⁡(X,L,𝐦)=max⁡{t≥0|μ∗​L−t​∑i=1rmi​Ei​is nef},\varepsilon(X,L;\mathbf{m})=\max\{\,t\geq 0\,|\,\mu^{*}L-t\,\sum_{i=1}^{r}m_{i}E_{i}\ \text{\rm{is nef}}\,\},

where μ:X~→X\mu:\widetilde{X}\rightarrow X is the blowing up along very general rr points on XX and E1,…,ErE_{1},\ldots,E_{r} are the exceptional divisors.

Proof.

The proof is essentially the same as that of [La, Theorem 5.1.17]. First, we show ε⁡(X,L,𝐦)≤max⁡{t≥0|μ∗​L−t​∑i=1rmi​Ei​is nef}\varepsilon(X,L;\mathbf{m})\leq\max\{\,t\geq 0\,|\,\mu^{*}L-t\,\sum_{i=1}^{r}m_{i}E_{i}\ \text{is nef}\,\}, i.e., μ∗​L−ε⁡(X,L,𝐦)​∑i=1rmi​Ei\mu^{*}L-\varepsilon(X,L;\mathbf{m})\sum_{i=1}^{r}m_{i}E_{i} is nef. Fix a curve C⊂XC\subset X and let C~⊂X~\widetilde{C}\subset\widetilde{X} be the strict transform of CC. It is enough to show (μ∗​L−ε⁡(X,L,𝐦)​∑i=1rmi​Ei).C~≥0(\mu^{*}L-\varepsilon(X,L;\mathbf{m})\sum_{i=1}^{r}m_{i}E_{i}).\widetilde{C}\geq 0. For each kk, the line bundle LkL^{k} separates ⌈sk​𝐦⌉\lceil s_{k}\mathbf{m}\rceil-jets at very general points p1,…,prp_{1},\ldots,p_{r}, where sk:=s⁡(k​L,𝐦)s_{k}:=s(kL;\mathbf{m}). Hence there exists an effective divisor D∈|Lk⊗⨂i𝔪pi⌈sk​mi⌉|D\in|L^{k}\otimes\bigotimes_{i}\mathfrak{m}_{p_{i}}^{\lceil s_{k}m_{i}\rceil}| such that DD does not contain CC. Thus it holds that

μ∗​L.C~=L.C\displaystyle\mu^{*}L.\widetilde{C}=L.C =k−1​D.C\displaystyle=k^{-1}D.C
≥k−1​∑imultpi⁡(D)⋅multpi⁡(C)\displaystyle\geq k^{-1}\sum_{i}\mult_{p_{i}}(D)\cdot\mult_{p_{i}}(C)
≥k−1​∑i⌈sk​mi⌉​multpi⁡(C)\displaystyle\geq k^{-1}\sum_{i}\lceil s_{k}m_{i}\rceil\mult_{p_{i}}(C)
≥k−1​∑isk​mi​multpi⁡(C)=k−1​sk​∑imi​Ei.C~,\displaystyle\geq k^{-1}\sum_{i}s_{k}m_{i}\mult_{p_{i}}(C)=k^{-1}s_{k}\sum_{i}m_{i}E_{i}.\widetilde{C},

where multpi\mult_{p_{i}} is the multiplicity at pip_{i}. By k→+∞k\rightarrow+\infty, we have μ∗​L.C~≥ε⁡(X,L,𝐦)​∑i=1rmi​Ei.C~\mu^{*}L.\widetilde{C}\geq\varepsilon(X,L;\mathbf{m})\sum_{i=1}^{r}m_{i}E_{i}.\widetilde{C}.

We show the opposite inequality. First, assume LL is ample. Let p1,…,prp_{1},\ldots,p_{r} be very general rr points in XX. Fix a rational number 0<t=a/b<max⁡{t≥0|μ∗​L−t​∑i=1rmi​Ei​is nef}0<t=a/b<\max\{\,t\geq 0\,|\,\mu^{*}L-t\,\sum_{i=1}^{r}m_{i}E_{i}\ \text{is nef}\,\} with positive integers a,ba,b. Then b​μ∗​L−a​∑i=1rmi​Eib\mu^{*}L-a\sum_{i=1}^{r}m_{i}E_{i} is an ample ℝ\mathbb{R}-line bundle on X~\widetilde{X}. Multiplying aa and bb by a sufficiently large positive integer, we may assume b​μ∗​L−∑i=1r⌈a​mi⌉​Eib\mu^{*}L-\sum_{i=1}^{r}\lceil am_{i}\rceil E_{i} is ample. By Serre’s vanishing theorem, there exists a natural number NN such that

H1​(X,k​b​L⊗⨂i𝔪pik​⌈a​mi⌉)=H1​(X~,k⁡(b​μ∗​L−∑i⌈a​mi⌉​Ei))=0H^{1}(X,kbL\otimes\bigotimes_{i}\mathfrak{m}_{p_{i}}^{k\lceil am_{i}\rceil})=H^{1}(\widetilde{X},k(b\mu^{*}L-\sum_{i}\lceil am_{i}\rceil E_{i}))=0

for every k≥Nk\geq N. This means k​b​LkbL separates (k⁡⌈a​m1⌉−1,…,k⁡⌈a​mr⌉−1)(k\lceil am_{1}\rceil-1,\ldots,k\lceil am_{r}\rceil-1)-jets at p1,…,prp_{1},\ldots,p_{r}, that is,

s⁡(k​b​L,𝐦)k​b≥mini⁡k​⌈a​mi⌉−1k​b​mi.\dfrac{s(kbL;\mathbf{m})}{kb}\geq\min_{i}\dfrac{k\lceil am_{i}\rceil-1}{kbm_{i}}.

By k→+∞k\rightarrow+\infty, we have

ε⁡(L,𝐦)≥limkmini⁡k​⌈a​mi⌉−1k​b​mi=ab=t.\varepsilon(L;\mathbf{m})\geq\lim_{k}\min_{i}\dfrac{k\lceil am_{i}\rceil-1}{kbm_{i}}=\frac{a}{b}=t.

By t→max⁡{t≥0|μ∗​L−t​∑i=1rmi​Ei​is nef}t\rightarrow\max\{\,t\geq 0\,|\,\mu^{*}L-t\,\sum_{i=1}^{r}m_{i}E_{i}\ \text{is nef}\,\}, we obtain ε⁡(L,𝐦)≥max⁡{t≥0|μ∗​L−t​∑i=1rmi​Ei​is nef}\varepsilon(L;\mathbf{m})\geq\max\{\,t\geq 0\,|\,\mu^{*}L-t\,\sum_{i=1}^{r}m_{i}E_{i}\ \text{is nef}\,\}.

Next we show the nef and big case. Since LL is nef and big, there exists an effective divisor EE on XX such that L−s​EL-sE is ample for any 0<s≪10<s\ll 1. Fix a rational number 0<s≪10<s\ll 1 and take a sufficiently divisible integer l∈ℤ+l\in{\mathbb{Z}}_{+} such that l​s∈ℤls\in\mathbb{Z}. Then ε⁡(l⁡(L−s​E),𝐦)≤ε⁡(l​L,𝐦)=l⋅ε⁡(L,𝐦)\varepsilon(l(L-sE);\mathbf{m})\leq\varepsilon(lL;\mathbf{m})=l\cdot\varepsilon(L;\mathbf{m}) holds by Remark 3.5 and Lemma 3.8 (1). Since l⁡(L−s​E)l(L-sE) is ample, we have

ε⁡(l⁡(L−s​E),𝐦)\displaystyle\varepsilon(l(L-sE);\mathbf{m}) =max⁡{t≥0|μ∗​(l⁡(L−s​E))−t​∑imi​Ei​is nef}\displaystyle=\max\{\,t\geq 0\,|\,\mu^{*}(l(L-sE))-t\,\sum_{i}m_{i}E_{i}\ \text{is nef}\,\}
=l⋅max⁡{t≥0|μ∗​(L−s​E)−t​∑imi​Ei​is nef}.\displaystyle=l\cdot\max\{\,t\geq 0\,|\,\mu^{*}(L-sE)-t\,\sum_{i}m_{i}E_{i}\ \text{is nef}\,\}.

Hence ε⁡(L,𝐦)≥max⁡{t≥0|μ∗​(L−s​E)−t​∑i=1rmi​Ei​is nef}\varepsilon(L;\mathbf{m})\geq\max\{\,t\geq 0\,|\,\mu^{*}(L-sE)-t\,\sum_{i=1}^{r}m_{i}E_{i}\ \text{is nef}\,\} holds. By s→0s\rightarrow 0, we have ε⁡(L,𝐦)≥max⁡{t≥0|μ∗​L−t​∑i=1rmi​Ei​is nef}\varepsilon(L;\mathbf{m})\geq\max\{\,t\geq 0\,|\,\mu^{*}L-t\,\sum_{i=1}^{r}m_{i}E_{i}\ \text{is nef}\,\}. ∎

For a line bundle LL on a projective variety XX, W∙={H0​(X,k​L)}kW_{\bullet}=\{H^{0}(X,kL)\}_{k} is birational if and only if LL is big. For a nef but not big line bundle LL on XX, we define ε⁡(X,L,𝐦):=max⁡{t≥0|μ∗​L−t​∑i=1rmi​Ei​is nef}=0\varepsilon(X,L;\mathbf{m}):=\max\{\,t\geq 0\,|\,\mu^{*}L-t\,\sum_{i=1}^{r}m_{i}E_{i}\ \text{is nef}\,\}=0.

For projective varieties, we can describe Seshadri constants of graded linear series by using those of nef line bundles as follows. This is a simple generalization of (some part of) [ELMNP, Propositions 6.4, 6.6], which treat ε⁡(L,1)\varepsilon(L;1) for a big line bundle LL, although their notations are slightly different.

Lemma 3.10.

Let W∙W_{\bullet} be a birational graded linear series associated to a line bundle LL on a projective variety XX. For each k>0k>0, set

Mk=μk∗​(k​L)−Fk,M_{k}=\mu_{k}^{*}(kL)-F_{k},

where μk:Xk→X\mu_{k}:X_{k}\rightarrow X is a resolution of the base ideal

𝔟k:=the image of​Wk⊗L−k→𝒪X\mathfrak{b}_{k}:=\text{\rm{the image of}}\,\ W_{k}\otimes L^{-k}\rightarrow\mathcal{O}_{X}

and 𝒪Xk​(−Fk):=μk−1​𝔟k\mathcal{O}_{X_{k}}(-F_{k}):=\mu_{k}^{-1}\mathfrak{b}_{k}. Set Mk=0M_{k}=0 if Wk=0W_{k}=0. Then it holds that

ε⁡(X,W∙,𝐦)=supk>0ε⁡(Xk,Mk,𝐦)k=limk>0ε⁡(Xk,Mk,𝐦)k.\varepsilon(X,W_{\bullet};\mathbf{m})=\sup_{k>0}\dfrac{\varepsilon(X_{k},M_{k};\mathbf{m})}{k}=\lim_{k>0}\dfrac{\varepsilon(X_{k},M_{k};\mathbf{m})}{k}.
Proof.

By definition, MkM_{k} is nef and ε⁡(Mk,𝐦)≥0\varepsilon(M_{k},\mathbf{m})\geq 0 for k>0k>0. To prove the existence of limkε⁡(Xk,Mk,𝐦)/k\lim_{k}\varepsilon(X_{k},M_{k};\mathbf{m})/k and the second equality in the above statement, it suffices to show the superadditivity of {ε⁡(Xk,Mk,𝐦)}k\{\varepsilon(X_{k},M_{k};\mathbf{m})\}_{k}, i.e.,

(†\dagger) ε⁡(Xk+l,Mk+l,𝐦)≥ε⁡(Xk,Mk,𝐦)+ε⁡(Xl,Ml,𝐦)\displaystyle\varepsilon(X_{k+l},M_{k+l},\mathbf{m})\geq\varepsilon(X_{k},M_{k};\mathbf{m})+\varepsilon(X_{l},M_{l};\mathbf{m})

for k,l>0k,l>0 such that Wk,Wl≠0W_{k},W_{l}\not=0.

To show (†\dagger), fix such k,l>0k,l>0. We can take a common resolution of 𝔟k,𝔟l\mathfrak{b}_{k},\mathfrak{b}_{l}, and 𝔟k+l\mathfrak{b}_{k+l}. Since Mk+l≥Mk+MlM_{k+l}\geq M_{k}+M_{l}, (†\dagger) follows from Lemmas 3.8 (3) or 3.9.

Next we show the first equality. Since μk∗​|Wk|⊂|Mk|\mu_{k}^{*}|W_{k}|\subset|M_{k}|, it holds that s⁡(Wk,𝐦)≤s⁡(Mk,𝐦)≤ε⁡(Mk,𝐦)s(W_{k};\mathbf{m})\leq s(M_{k};\mathbf{m})\leq\varepsilon(M_{k};\mathbf{m}) for any kk. Thus we have

ε⁡(X,W∙,𝐦)=lims⁡(Wk,𝐦)k≤limε⁡(Mk,𝐦)k.\varepsilon(X,W_{\bullet};\mathbf{m})=\lim\dfrac{s(W_{k};\mathbf{m})}{k}\leq\lim\dfrac{\varepsilon(M_{k};\mathbf{m})}{k}.

To show the opposite inequality, we use Lemma 3.9. Since W∙W_{\bullet} is birational, the morphism φk:Xk→ℙdim|Wk|\varphi_{k}:X_{k}\rightarrow\mathbb{P}^{\dim|W_{k}|} defined by μk∗​|Wk|\mu_{k}^{*}|W_{k}| is birational onto its image for k≫0k\gg 0. Denote the image of φk\varphi_{k} by YkY_{k}. By Lemma 3.9, ε⁡(Xk,Mk,𝐦)=ε⁡(Yk,𝒪Yk​(1),𝐦)\varepsilon(X_{k},M_{k};\mathbf{m})=\varepsilon(Y_{k},\mathcal{O}_{Y_{k}}(1);\mathbf{m}) holds because φk\varphi_{k} is birational. Furthermore Wkl=H0​(Yk,𝒪Yk​(l))W_{k}^{l}=H^{0}(Y_{k},\mathcal{O}_{Y_{k}}(l)) for l≫0l\gg 0, where WklW_{k}^{l} is the image of Wk⊗l→Wk​lW_{k}^{\otimes l}\rightarrow W_{kl}. This implies s⁡(𝒪Yk​(l),𝐦)=s⁡(Wkl,𝐦)≤s⁡(Wk​l,𝐦)s(\mathcal{O}_{Y_{k}}(l);\mathbf{m})=s(W_{k}^{l};\mathbf{m})\leq s(W_{kl};\mathbf{m}) for l≫0l\gg 0. Thus we have

ε⁡(Xk,Mk,𝐦)k\displaystyle\dfrac{\varepsilon(X_{k},M_{k};\mathbf{m})}{k} =ε⁡(Yk,𝒪Yk​(1),𝐦)k\displaystyle=\dfrac{\varepsilon(Y_{k},\mathcal{O}_{Y_{k}}(1);\mathbf{m})}{k}
=1k​limls​(𝒪Yk​(l),𝐦)l\displaystyle=\frac{1}{k}\lim_{l}\dfrac{s(\mathcal{O}_{Y_{k}}(l);\mathbf{m})}{l}
≤lims⁡(Wk​l,𝐦)k​l=ε⁡(W∙,𝐦).∎\displaystyle\leq\lim\dfrac{s(W_{kl};\mathbf{m})}{kl}=\varepsilon(W_{\bullet};\mathbf{m}).\qed

4. Monomial graded linear series on (ℂ×)n(\mathbb{C}^{\times})^{n}

Definition 4.1.

Let nn be a positive integer. For a subset S⊂ℝnS\subset\mathbb{R}^{n}, we set

VS:=⨁u∈S∩ℤnℂ​xu,V_{S}:=\bigoplus_{u\in S\cap\mathbb{Z}^{n}}\mathbb{C}x^{u},

which is a subspace of ⨁u∈ℤnℂ​xu=H0​((ℂ×)n,𝒪(ℂ×)n).\bigoplus_{u\in\mathbb{Z}^{n}}\mathbb{C}x^{u}=H^{0}((\mathbb{C}^{\times})^{n},\mathcal{O}_{(\mathbb{C}^{\times})^{n}}).

For a convex set Δ\Delta in ℝn\mathbb{R}^{n}, we define the monomial graded linear series WΔ,∙W_{\Delta,\bullet} associated to 𝒪(ℂ×)n\mathcal{O}_{(\mathbb{C}^{\times})^{n}} by

WΔ,k:=Vk​Δ⊂H0​((ℂ×)n,𝒪(ℂ×)n).W_{\Delta,k}:=V_{k\Delta}\subset H^{0}((\mathbb{C}^{\times})^{n},\mathcal{O}_{(\mathbb{C}^{\times})^{n}}).

It is easy to see that WΔ,∙W_{\Delta,\bullet} is birational if and only if dimΔ=n\dim\Delta=n.

Definition 4.2.

For an nn-dimensional convex set Δ⊂ℝn\Delta\subset\mathbb{R}^{n} and 𝐦∈ℝ+r\mathbf{m}\in{\mathbb{R}}_{+}^{r}, we define ε⁡(Δ,𝐦):=ε⁡(WΔ,∙,𝐦)∈ℝ+\varepsilon(\Delta;\mathbf{m}):=\varepsilon(W_{\Delta,\bullet},\mathbf{m})\in{\mathbb{R}}_{+}.

Remark 4.3.

For an integral polytope Δ⊂ℝn\Delta\subset\mathbb{R}^{n} of dimension nn, clearly ε⁡(Δ,𝐦)=ε⁡(XΔ,LΔ,𝐦)\varepsilon(\Delta;\mathbf{m})=\varepsilon(X_{\Delta},L_{\Delta};\mathbf{m}) holds, where (XΔ,LΔ)=(Proj⨁kVk​Δ,𝒪(1))(X_{\Delta},L_{\Delta})=(\Proj\bigoplus_{k}V_{k\Delta},\mathcal{O}(1)) is the polarized toric variety corresponding to Δ\Delta.

We show some basic properties of ε⁡(Δ,𝐦)\varepsilon(\Delta;\mathbf{m}) in this section.

Lemma 4.4.

The following hold for subsets S1,S2S_{1},S_{2} and nn-dimensional convex sets Δ1,Δ2\Delta_{1},\Delta_{2} in ℝn\mathbb{R}^{n} such that S1⊂S2,Δ1⊂Δ2S_{1}\subset S_{2},\,\Delta_{1}\subset\Delta_{2}.

  • (1)

    s⁡(VS1,𝐦)≤s⁡(VS2,𝐦),ε⁡(Δ1,𝐦)≤ε⁡(Δ2,𝐦)s(V_{S_{1}};\mathbf{m})\leq s(V_{S_{2}};\mathbf{m}),\,\varepsilon(\Delta_{1};\mathbf{m})\leq\varepsilon(\Delta_{2};\mathbf{m}).

(1) is clear. (2) immediately follows from the diagram

To show (3), choose sufficiently divisible l∈ℤ+l\in{\mathbb{Z}}_{+} such that l​t∈ℤlt\in\mathbb{Z} and l​u∈ℤnlu\in\mathbb{Z}^{n}. Then we have

=limks⁡(Vk​l​t​Δ1,𝐦)k​l\displaystyle=\lim_{k}\dfrac{s(V_{klt\Delta_{1}};\mathbf{m})}{kl}

=limks⁡(Vk​l​Δ1,𝐦)k​l=ε⁡(Δ1,𝐦).\displaystyle=\lim_{k}\dfrac{s(V_{kl\Delta_{1}};\mathbf{m})}{kl}=\varepsilon(\Delta_{1};\mathbf{m}).

Lemma 4.5.

For an nn-dimensional convex set Δ⊂ℝn\Delta\subset\mathbb{R}^{n}, ε⁡(Δ,𝐦)=ε⁡(Δ∘,𝐦)\varepsilon(\Delta;\mathbf{m})=\varepsilon(\Delta^{\circ};\mathbf{m}) holds.

For an nn-dimensional convex set Δ⊂ℝn\Delta\subset\mathbb{R}^{n}, u∈ℝnu\in\mathbb{R}^{n}, and t∈ℝ+t\in{\mathbb{R}}_{+}, it holds that

For t1,t2∈ℚt_{1},t_{2}\in\mathbb{Q} such that 0<t1≤t≤t20<t_{1}\leq t\leq t_{2}, we have inclusions t1​(Δ−u′)⊂t⁡(Δ−u′)⊂t2​(Δ−u′)t_{1}(\Delta-u^{\prime})\subset t(\Delta-u^{\prime})\subset t_{2}(\Delta-u^{\prime}). Thus it holds that

5. Okounkov bodies and Seshadri constants

In this section, we prove Theorem 1.3.

5.1. Preliminary

For a subsemigroup Γ\Gamma in ℕ×ℕn\mathbb{N}\times\mathbb{N}^{n} and k∈ℕk\in\mathbb{N}, set

Δ⁡(Γ)\displaystyle\Delta(\Gamma) =Σ⁡(Γ)∩({1}×ℝn),\displaystyle=\Sigma(\Gamma)\cap(\{1\}\times\mathbb{R}^{n}),
Γk\displaystyle\Gamma_{k} =Γ∩({k}×ℕn).\displaystyle=\Gamma\cap(\{k\}\times\mathbb{N}^{n}).

Recall that Σ⁡(Γ)\Sigma(\Gamma) is the closed convex cone in ℝ×ℝn\mathbb{R}\times\mathbb{R}^{n} spanned by Γ\Gamma. We regard Δ⁡(Γ)\Delta(\Gamma) and Γk\Gamma_{k} as subsets in ℝn\mathbb{R}^{n} and ℕn\mathbb{N}^{n} respectively in a natural way.

Definition 5.1.

For a semigroup Γ\Gamma in ℕ×ℕn\mathbb{N}\times\mathbb{N}^{n}, we define a graded linear series W​(Γ)∙W(\Gamma)_{\bullet} on (ℂ×)n(\mathbb{C}^{\times})^{n} associated to 𝒪(ℂ×)n\mathcal{O}_{(\mathbb{C}^{\times})^{n}} by W​(Γ)k:=VΓk.W(\Gamma)_{k}:=V_{\Gamma_{k}}.

The birationality of W​(Γ)∙W(\Gamma)_{\bullet} is interpreted as the following conditions of Γ\Gamma.

Definition 5.2.

A semigroup Γ\Gamma in ℕ×ℕn\mathbb{N}\times\mathbb{N}^{n} is birational if

  • i)

    Γ0={0}∈ℕn\Gamma_{0}=\{0\}\in\mathbb{N}^{n},

  • ii)

    Γ\Gamma generates ℤ×ℤn\mathbb{Z}\times\mathbb{Z}^{n} as a group.

These conditions are (2.3) and (2,5) in [LM] respectively. It is easy to check that Γ\Gamma is birational if and only if so is the graded linear series W​(Γ)∙W(\Gamma)_{\bullet}.

Let >> be a monomial order on ℕn\mathbb{N}^{n}, i.e., >> is a total order on ℕn\mathbb{N}^{n} such that (i) for every u∈ℕn∖0u\in\mathbb{N}^{n}\setminus 0, u>0u>0 holds, and (ii) if v>uv>u and w∈ℕnw\in\mathbb{N}^{n}, then w+v>w+uw+v>w+u. In this paper, v>uv>u does not contain the case v=uv=u.

Let XX be a variety of dimension nn and z=(z1,…,zn)z=(z_{1},\ldots,z_{n}) a local coordinate system at a smooth point p∈Xp\in X. For a birational graded linear series W∙W_{\bullet} associated to a line bundle LL on XX, we can define a semigroup ΓW∙=ΓW∙,z,>⊂ℕ×ℕn\Gamma_{W_{\bullet}}=\Gamma_{W_{\bullet},z,>}\subset\mathbb{N}\times\mathbb{N}^{n} by using ν=νz,>:𝒪X,p∖0→ℕn\nu=\nu_{z,>}:\mathcal{O}_{X,p}\setminus 0\rightarrow\mathbb{N}^{n} as in Introduction.

In [LM, Lemma 2.12], they assume that W∙W_{\bullet} satisfies “Condition (C)”, which seems to be a slightly stronger condition than being birational(= Condition (B) in [LM]), to show that ΓW∙,z,>\Gamma_{W_{\bullet},z,>} generates ℤ×ℤn\mathbb{Z}\times\mathbb{Z}^{n} as a group for any zz. But we can show that it is enough to assume W∙W_{\bullet} is birational.

Lemma 5.3.

Let W∙W_{\bullet} be a birational graded linear series associated to a line bundle LL on a variety XX. Then ΓW∙,z,>\Gamma_{W_{\bullet},z,>} is birational for any local coordinate system zz at any smooth point p∈Xp\in X and any monomial order >> on ℕn\mathbb{N}^{n}.

Proof.

The condition i) in Definition 5.2 is clearly satisfied. Thus it is enough to show that ΓW∙\Gamma_{W_{\bullet}} generates ℤ×ℤn\mathbb{Z}\times\mathbb{Z}^{n} as a group. Fix k≫0k\gg 0. Then the function field K⁡(X)K(X) is generated by {f/g∈K(X)|f,g∈Wk,g≠0}\{\,f/g\in K(X)\,|\,f,g\in W_{k},g\not=0\} over ℂ\mathbb{C} because W∙W_{\bullet} is birational. Hence for any F∈K⁡(X)∖{0}F\in K(X)\setminus\{0\}, we can write F=G/HF=G/H, where G,HG,H are written as some polynomials over ℂ\mathbb{C} of some elements in {f/g∈K(X)|f,g∈Wk,g≠0}\{\,f/g\in K(X)\,|\,f,g\in W_{k},g\not=0\}. Therefore we can write F=G′/H′F=G^{\prime}/H^{\prime} for some G′,H′∈Wk​lG^{\prime},H^{\prime}\in W_{kl} for some l∈ℤ+l\in{\mathbb{Z}}_{+}. Thus ν⁡(F)=ν⁡(G′)−ν⁡(H′)∈ν⁡(Wk​l)−ν⁡(Wk​l)⊂ℤn.\nu(F)=\nu(G^{\prime})-\nu(H^{\prime})\in\nu(W_{kl})-\nu(W_{kl})\subset\mathbb{Z}^{n}. Since the valuation ν:K⁡(X)∖{0}→ℤn\nu:K(X)\setminus\{0\}\rightarrow\mathbb{Z}^{n} is surjective (note that ν\nu is naturally extended to K⁡(X)∖{0}K(X)\setminus\{0\}), the group ℤn\mathbb{Z}^{n} is generated by {ν⁡(Wk​l)−ν⁡(Wk​l)}l∈ℕ\{\nu(W_{kl})-\nu(W_{kl})\}_{l\in\mathbb{N}}. Thus the subgroup {0}×ℤn\{0\}\times\mathbb{Z}^{n} in ℤ×ℤn\mathbb{Z}\times\mathbb{Z}^{n} is generated by {0}×{ν⁡(Wk​l)−ν⁡(Wk​l)}l⊂ΓW∙−ΓW∙\{0\}\times\{\nu(W_{kl})-\nu(W_{kl})\}_{l}\subset\Gamma_{W_{\bullet}}-\Gamma_{W_{\bullet}}.

On the other hand, sk∈Wk∖{0}s_{k}\in W_{k}\setminus\{0\} and sk+1∈Wk+1∖{0}s_{k+1}\in W_{k+1}\setminus\{0\} induce the element (1,ν⁡(sk+1)−ν⁡(sk))∈ΓW∙−ΓW∙⊂ℤ×ℤn(1,\nu(s_{k+1})-\nu(s_{k}))\in\Gamma_{W_{\bullet}}-\Gamma_{W_{\bullet}}\subset\mathbb{Z}\times\mathbb{Z}^{n}. Since the group ℤ×ℤn\mathbb{Z}\times\mathbb{Z}^{n} is generated by {0}×ℤn\{0\}\times\mathbb{Z}^{n} and (1,ν⁡(sk+1)−ν⁡(sk))(1,\nu(s_{k+1})-\nu(s_{k})), the semigroup ΓW∙\Gamma_{W_{\bullet}} generates ℤ×ℤn\mathbb{Z}\times\mathbb{Z}^{n} as a group. ∎

Let W∙W_{\bullet} be a birational graded linear series associated to a line bundle LL on XX. We define the Okounkov body Δ⁡(W∙)=Δz,>​(W∙)\Delta(W_{\bullet})=\Delta_{z,>}(W_{\bullet}) of W∙W_{\bullet} with respect to zz and >> as in Introduction. That is, Δz,>​(W∙)=Δ⁡(ΓW∙,z,>)\Delta_{z,>}(W_{\bullet})=\Delta(\Gamma_{W_{\bullet},z,>}). Thus Δ⁡(W∙)\Delta(W_{\bullet}) is an nn-dimensional closed convex set in ℝn\mathbb{R}^{n} because ΓW∙\Gamma_{W_{\bullet}} is birational by Lemma 5.3.

The following lemma is similar to [An, Lemma 5.2].

Lemma 5.4.

For a monomial order >> on ℕn\mathbb{N}^{n} and a finite set SS in ℕn\mathbb{N}^{n}, there exists α∈ℤ+n\alpha\in{\mathbb{Z}}_{+}^{n} satisfying the following: For u∈Su\in S and v∈ℕnv\in\mathbb{N}^{n} such that v>uv>u, it holds that α⋅v>α⋅u\alpha\cdot v>\alpha\cdot u, where α⋅u,α⋅v\alpha\cdot u,\,\alpha\cdot v are the usual inner products.

Proof.

For each u∈Su\in S, set Su={v∈ℕn|v>u}S_{u}=\{v\in\mathbb{N}^{n}\,|\,v>u\}. Let IuI_{u} be the ideal in the polynomial ring ℂ⁡[ℕn]=ℂ⁡[x1,…,xn]\mathbb{C}[\mathbb{N}^{n}]=\mathbb{C}[x_{1},\ldots,x_{n}] generated by {xv|v∈Su}\{\,x^{v}\,|\,v\in S_{u}\}. By Hilbert’s basis theorem, IuI_{u} is generated by xvu​1,…,xvu​kux^{v_{u1}},\ldots,x^{v_{uk_{u}}} for some ku∈ℕk_{u}\in\mathbb{N} and vu​1,…,vu​ku∈Suv_{u1},\ldots,v_{uk_{u}}\in S_{u}. Therefore any v∈Suv\in S_{u} is contained in vu​j+ℕnv_{uj}+\mathbb{N}^{n} for some jj.

We use the following result by Robbiano.

Theorem 5.5 ([Ro, Theorem 2.5]).

For a monomial order >> on ℕn\mathbb{N}^{n}, there exist an integer s∈{1,…,n}s\in\{1,\ldots,n\} and u1,…,us∈ℝnu_{1},...,u_{s}\in\mathbb{R}^{n} which satisfy the following: For u,v∈ℕnu,v\in\mathbb{N}^{n}, v>uv>u if and only if π(v)>lexπ(u)\pi(v)>_{\lex}\pi(u), where

π:ℕn→ℝs;u↦(u1⋅u,…,us⋅u)\pi:\mathbb{N}^{n}\rightarrow\mathbb{R}^{s};\ u\mapsto(u_{1}\cdot u,\ldots,u_{s}\cdot u)

and >lex>_{\lex} is the lexicographic order on ℝs\mathbb{R}^{s}.

Let e1,…,ene_{1},\ldots,e_{n} be the standard basis of ℤn\mathbb{Z}^{n} and consider the above u1,…,usu_{1},\ldots,u_{s} and π\pi. For any γ>lexδ\gamma>_{\lex}\delta in ℝs\mathbb{R}^{s}, the following holds from the definition of the lexicographic order: For β=(β1,…,βs)∈ℝ+s\beta=(\beta_{1},\ldots,\beta_{s})\in{\mathbb{R}}_{+}^{s} such that β1≫⋯≫βs\beta_{1}\gg\cdots\gg\beta_{s}, we have β⋅γ>β⋅δ\beta\cdot\gamma>\beta\cdot\delta.

Hence we can take β∈ℝ+s\beta\in{\mathbb{R}}_{+}^{s} such that

  • •

    β⋅π⁡(ei)>0\beta\cdot\pi(e_{i})>0 for 1≤i≤n1\leq i\leq n,

  • •

    β⋅π⁡(vu​j)>β⋅π⁡(u)\beta\cdot\pi(v_{uj})>\beta\cdot\pi(u) for u∈Su\in S and 1≤j≤ku1\leq j\leq k_{u},

since π(ei)>lexπ(0)=0\pi(e_{i})>_{\lex}\pi(0)=0 and π(vu​j)>lexπ(u)\pi(v_{uj})>_{\lex}\pi(u) (we can take common β\beta because SS is a finite set). Since β⋅π⁡(u′)=(β1​u1+⋯+βs​us)⋅u′\beta\cdot\pi(u^{\prime})=(\beta_{1}u_{1}+\cdots+\beta_{s}u_{s})\cdot u^{\prime} for u′∈ℕnu^{\prime}\in\mathbb{N}^{n}, we have

(∗*) α′⋅ei>0,α′⋅vu​j>α′⋅u\displaystyle\alpha^{\prime}\cdot e_{i}>0,\quad\alpha^{\prime}\cdot v_{uj}>\alpha^{\prime}\cdot u

for 1≤i≤n,u∈S1\leq i\leq n,u\in S and 1≤j≤ku1\leq j\leq k_{u} if we take α′∈ℚn\alpha^{\prime}\in\mathbb{Q}^{n} sufficiently close to β1​u1+⋯+βs​us\beta_{1}u_{1}+\cdots+\beta_{s}u_{s}. Set α:=N​α′∈ℤn\alpha:=N\alpha^{\prime}\in\mathbb{Z}^{n} for a sufficiently divisible positive integer NN. By (∗)(*), it follows that α∈ℤ+n\alpha\in{\mathbb{Z}}_{+}^{n} and α⋅vu​j>α⋅u\alpha\cdot v_{uj}>\alpha\cdot u for u∈Su\in S and jj.

We show this α\alpha satisfies the condition in the statement of this lemma. Fix u∈Su\in S and v∈ℕnv\in\mathbb{N}^{n} such that v>uv>u, i.e., v∈Suv\in S_{u}. Then v∈vu​j+ℕnv\in v_{uj}+\mathbb{N}^{n} for some 1≤j≤ku1\leq j\leq k_{u}. Thus we have α⋅v=α⋅vu​j+α⋅(v−vu​j)≥α⋅vu​j>α⋅u\alpha\cdot v=\alpha\cdot v_{uj}+\alpha\cdot(v-v_{uj})\geq\alpha\cdot v_{uj}>\alpha\cdot u. ∎

5.2. Proof of Theorem 1.3

Since Seshadri constants are lower semicontinuous (cf. [La, Example 5.1.11]), degenerations are useful to bound Seshadri constants from below. For example, Biran [Bi] degenerates varieties to reducible schemes, and gives lower bounds of (multi-point) Seshadri constants on ℙ2\mathbb{P}^{2}. In [It], the author uses toric degenerations to obtain lower bounds of Seshadri constants on some non-toric varieties.

We also use degenerations to prove Theorem 1.3. Although we would like to degenerate ⨁kWk\bigoplus_{k}W_{k} to ℂ⁡[ΓW∙]=⨁kVν⁡(Wk)\mathbb{C}[\Gamma_{W_{\bullet}}]=\bigoplus_{k}V_{\nu(W_{k})}, the semigroup ΓW∙\Gamma_{W_{\bullet}} is not finitely generated in general, even if ⨁kWk\bigoplus_{k}W_{k} is finitely generated. Instead, we degenerate WkW_{k} to Vν⁡(Wk)V_{\nu(W_{k})} for each kk separately. Then we can use the lower semicontinuity of jet separation, as in [CM]. This is the reason why we define Seshadri constants in terms of jet separation.

First, we show that the Seshadri constants of W​(Γ)∙W(\Gamma)_{\bullet} and WΔ⁡(Γ),∙W_{\Delta(\Gamma),\bullet} coincide for a birational semigroup Γ\Gamma.

Lemma 5.6.

For a birational semigroup Γ⊂ℕ×ℕn\Gamma\subset\mathbb{N}\times\mathbb{N}^{n} and 𝐦∈ℝ+r\mathbf{m}\in{\mathbb{R}}_{+}^{r}, we have ε⁡(Δ⁡(Γ),𝐦)=ε⁡(W​(Γ)∙,𝐦)\varepsilon(\Delta(\Gamma);\mathbf{m})=\varepsilon(W(\Gamma)_{\bullet};\mathbf{m}).

Proof.

By definition, it holds that

ε⁡(Δ⁡(Γ),𝐦)=lims⁡(Vk​Δ​(Γ),𝐦)k,ε⁡(W​(Γ)∙,𝐦)=lims⁡(VΓk,𝐦)k.\varepsilon(\Delta(\Gamma);\mathbf{m})=\lim\dfrac{s(V_{k\Delta(\Gamma)};\mathbf{m})}{k},\quad\varepsilon(W(\Gamma)_{\bullet};\mathbf{m})=\lim\dfrac{s(V_{\Gamma_{k}};\mathbf{m})}{k}.

Since Γk\Gamma_{k} is contained in k​Δ​(Γ)k\Delta(\Gamma) for any kk, ε⁡(Δ⁡(Γ),𝐦)≥ε⁡(W​(Γ)∙,𝐦)\varepsilon(\Delta(\Gamma);\mathbf{m})\geq\varepsilon(W(\Gamma)_{\bullet};\mathbf{m}) is clear. Hence it is enough to show the opposite inequality.

When Γ\Gamma is finitely generated, there exists u~=(l,u)∈Γ⊂ℕ×ℕn\tilde{u}=(l,u)\in\Gamma\subset\mathbb{N}\times\mathbb{N}^{n} such that (Σ⁡(Γ)+u~)∩(ℕ×ℕn)⊂Γ(\Sigma(\Gamma)+\tilde{u})\cap(\mathbb{N}\times\mathbb{N}^{n})\subset\Gamma by [Kh, §3, Proposition 3] (see also [LM, Subsection 2.1]). This induces (k​Δ​(Γ)∩ℕn)+u⊂Γk+l(k\Delta(\Gamma)\cap\mathbb{N}^{n})+u\subset\Gamma_{k+l}, from which we have s⁡(Vk​Δ​(Γ),𝐦)=s⁡(V(k​Δ​(Γ)∩ℕn)+u,𝐦)≤s⁡(VΓk+l,𝐦)s(V_{k\Delta(\Gamma)};\mathbf{m})=s(V_{(k\Delta(\Gamma)\cap\mathbb{N}^{n})+u};\mathbf{m})\leq s(V_{\Gamma_{k+l}};\mathbf{m}). Thus we obtain

ε⁡(W​(Γ)∙,𝐦)=limks⁡(VΓk,𝐦)k\displaystyle\varepsilon(W(\Gamma)_{\bullet};\mathbf{m})=\lim_{k}\dfrac{s(V_{\Gamma_{k}};\mathbf{m})}{k} =limks⁡(VΓk+l,𝐦)k\displaystyle=\lim_{k}\dfrac{s(V_{\Gamma_{k+l}};\mathbf{m})}{k}
≥limks⁡(Vk​Δ​(Γ),𝐦)k=ε⁡(Δ⁡(Γ),𝐦).\displaystyle\geq\lim_{k}\dfrac{s(V_{k\Delta(\Gamma)};\mathbf{m})}{k}=\varepsilon(\Delta(\Gamma);\mathbf{m}).

In the general case, we take an increasing sequence Γ1⊂Γ2⊂⋯⊂Γ\Gamma^{1}\subset\Gamma^{2}\subset\cdots\subset\Gamma such that each Γi\Gamma^{i} is a finitely generated birational subsemigroup of Γ\Gamma and ⋃i≥1Γi=Γ\bigcup_{i\geq 1}\Gamma^{i}=\Gamma. Then it is easy to show ⋃iΔ​(Γi)∘=Δ​(Γ)∘\bigcup_{i}\Delta(\Gamma^{i})^{\circ}=\Delta(\Gamma)^{\circ}. By Lemmas 4.5 and 4.7, we have

ε⁡(Δ⁡(Γ),𝐦)=ε⁡(Δ​(Γ)∘,𝐦)=limε⁡(Δ​(Γi)∘,𝐦)=limε⁡(Δ⁡(Γi),𝐦).\varepsilon(\Delta(\Gamma);\mathbf{m})=\varepsilon(\Delta(\Gamma)^{\circ};\mathbf{m})=\lim\varepsilon(\Delta(\Gamma^{i})^{\circ};\mathbf{m})=\lim\varepsilon(\Delta(\Gamma^{i});\mathbf{m}).

Since each Γi\Gamma^{i} is finitely generated, we can apply the first part of the proof of this lemma. Hence we have

ε⁡(Δ⁡(Γi),𝐦)=ε⁡(W​(Γi)∙,𝐦)≤ε⁡(W​(Γ)∙,𝐦).\varepsilon(\Delta(\Gamma^{i});\mathbf{m})=\varepsilon(W(\Gamma^{i})_{\bullet};\mathbf{m})\leq\varepsilon(W(\Gamma)_{\bullet};\mathbf{m}).

Thus we obtain ε⁡(Δ⁡(Γ),𝐦)=limε⁡(Δ⁡(Γi),𝐦)≤ε⁡(W​(Γ)∙,𝐦)\varepsilon(\Delta(\Gamma);\mathbf{m})=\lim\varepsilon(\Delta(\Gamma^{i});\mathbf{m})\leq\varepsilon(W(\Gamma)_{\bullet};\mathbf{m}). ∎

Broadly speaking, the geometrical meaning of Lemma 5.6 is that Seshadri constants of ample line bundles (on non-normal toric varieties) at very general points do not change by normalizations. In fact, when Γ\Gamma is finitely generated, (Proj⨁kWΔ⁡(Γ),k,𝒪(1))=(Projℂ[Σ(Γ)∩(ℕ×ℕn)],𝒪(1))(\Proj\bigoplus_{k}W_{\Delta(\Gamma),k},\mathcal{O}(1))=(\Proj\mathbb{C}[\Sigma(\Gamma)\cap(\mathbb{N}\times\mathbb{N}^{n})],\mathcal{O}(1)) is nothing but the normalization of the toric variety (Proj⨁kW(Γ)k,𝒪(1))=(Projℂ[Γ],𝒪(1))(\Proj\bigoplus_{k}W(\Gamma)_{k},\mathcal{O}(1))=(\Proj\mathbb{C}[\Gamma],\mathcal{O}(1)).

Now we show the key proposition by using degeneration of global sections as [CM]. Roughly speaking, this proposition states that W⊂H0​(X,L)W\subset H^{0}(X,L) generically separates no less jets than Vν⁡(W)V_{\nu(W)}.

Proposition 5.7.

Let LL be a line bundle on an nn-dimensional variety XX. Let ν=νz,>\nu=\nu_{z,>} be the valuation map defined by a local coordinate system z=(z1,…,zn)z=(z_{1},\ldots,z_{n}) at a smooth point p∈Xp\in X and a monomial order >> on ℕn\mathbb{N}^{n}. Then s⁡(W,𝐦)≥s⁡(Vν⁡(W),𝐦)s(W;\mathbf{m})\geq s(V_{\nu(W)};\mathbf{m}) holds for any subspace WW of H0​(X,L)H^{0}(X,L) and any 𝐦∈ℝ+r\mathbf{m}\in{\mathbb{R}}_{+}^{r}.

Proof.

By considering an increasing sequence of finite dimensional subspaces in WW, we may assume dimW<+∞\dim W<+\infty.

Let π:U→ℂn\pi:U\rightarrow\mathbb{C}^{n} be the étale morphism defined by z1,…,znz_{1},\ldots,z_{n} in an open neighborhood U⊂XU\subset X of pp. By the morphism π\pi, we can identify 𝒪X,pa​n\mathcal{O}_{X,p}^{an} with 𝒪ℂn,0a​n=ℂ⁡{x1,…,xn}\mathcal{O}^{an}_{\mathbb{C}^{n},0}=\mathbb{C}\{x_{1},\ldots,x_{n}\}, where x1,…,xnx_{1},\ldots,x_{n} are the coordinates on ℂn\mathbb{C}^{n} such that π∗​xi=zi\pi^{*}x_{i}=z_{i}. Then we can regard WW as a subspace of ℂ⁡{x1,…,xn}\mathbb{C}\{x_{1},\ldots,x_{n}\} by W↪Lp≅𝒪X,p↪ℂ⁡{x1,…,xn}W\hookrightarrow L_{p}\cong\mathcal{O}_{X,p}\hookrightarrow\mathbb{C}\{x_{1},\ldots,x_{n}\}. Note that ν\nu is extended to 𝒪X,pa​n∖{0}=ℂ⁡{x1,…,xn}∖{0}→ℕn\mathcal{O}_{X,p}^{an}\setminus\{0\}=\mathbb{C}\{x_{1},\ldots,x_{n}\}\setminus\{0\}\rightarrow\mathbb{N}^{n} naturally.

Choose and fix fu∈ν−1​(u)∩Wf_{u}\in\nu^{-1}(u)\cap W for each u∈ν⁡(W)u\in\nu(W). Then it holds that V=⨁u∈ν⁡(W)ℂ​fuV=\bigoplus_{u\in\nu(W)}\mathbb{C}f_{u} because #ν⁡(W)=dimW\nu(W)=\dim W (cf. [LM] or [BC]). Since ν⁡(W)\nu(W) is a finite set, there exists α∈ℤ+n\alpha\in{\mathbb{Z}}_{+}^{n} satisfying the following by Lemma 5.4; if v>uv>u for u∈ν⁡(W)u\in\nu(W) and v∈ℕnv\in\mathbb{N}^{n}, it holds that α⋅v>α⋅u\alpha\cdot v>\alpha\cdot u.

The vector α\alpha induces the action ∘\circ of ℂ×\mathbb{C}^{\times} on ℂ⁡{x1,…,xn}\mathbb{C}\{x_{1},\ldots,x_{n}\} by t∘xu:=tα⋅u​xut\circ x^{u}:=t^{\alpha\cdot u}x^{u} for t∈ℂ×t\in\mathbb{C}^{\times} and u∈ℕnu\in\mathbb{N}^{n}. For fu=∑vcu​v​zv=∑vcu​v​xvf_{u}=\sum_{v}c_{uv}z^{v}=\sum_{v}c_{uv}x^{v} (note we identify ziz_{i} and xix_{i}), the regular function

t∘futα⋅u=t−α⋅u∑vcu​vtα⋅vxv=∑vcu​vtα⋅v−α⋅uxv\dfrac{t\circ f_{u}}{t^{\alpha\cdot u}}=t^{-\alpha\cdot u}\sum_{v}c_{uv}t^{\alpha\cdot v}x^{v}=\sum_{v}c_{uv}t^{\alpha\cdot v-\alpha\cdot u}x^{v}

on a neighborhood of ℂ××{0}\mathbb{C}^{\times}\times\{0\} (in ℂ××ℂn\mathbb{C}^{\times}\times\mathbb{C}^{n}) is naturally extended to a regular function on a neighborhood 𝒰\mathcal{U} of ℂ×{0}\mathbb{C}\times\{0\}. Note that α⋅v−α⋅u≥0\alpha\cdot v-\alpha\cdot u\geq 0 if cu​v≠0c_{uv}\not=0. We denote the regular function by FuF_{u}. Set 𝒲=⨁u∈ν⁡(W)ℂ​Fu\mathcal{W}=\bigoplus_{u\in\nu(W)}\mathbb{C}F_{u}.

We prove this proposition only for r=1r=1. When r>1r>1, the proof is similar. Thus we leave the details to the reader.

Choose a very general section σ\sigma of the projection 𝒰→ℂ\mathcal{U}\rightarrow\mathbb{C} onto the first factor. Let ℐ\mathcal{I} be the ideal sheaf corresponding to σ⁡(ℂ)\sigma(\mathbb{C}) on 𝒰⊂ℂ×ℂn\mathcal{U}\subset\mathbb{C}\times\mathbb{C}^{n}. For s≥0s\geq 0, we consider the map

of flat sheaves over ℂ\mathbb{C}. For t∈ℂt\in\mathbb{C}, we write Wt:=𝒲⊗ℂ⁡{t}|{t}×ℂnW_{t}:=\mathcal{W}\otimes\mathbb{C}\{t\}|_{\{t\}\times\mathbb{C}^{n}} and

ϕt:=ϕ|{t}×ℂn:Wt→𝒪𝒰a​n/ℐs+1|{t}×ℂn=𝒪ℂn/𝔪σ⁡(t)s+1.\phi_{t}:=\phi|_{\{t\}\times\mathbb{C}^{n}}:W_{t}\rightarrow\mathcal{O}^{an}_{\mathcal{U}}/\mathcal{I}^{s+1}|_{\{t\}\times\mathbb{C}^{n}}=\mathcal{O}_{\mathbb{C}^{n}}/\mathfrak{m}_{\sigma(t)}^{s+1}.

for tt in a neighborhood of 00. Since there is a natural identification of WtW_{t} and WW for t∈ℂ×t\in\mathbb{C}^{\times} by the action ∘\circ, we have s⁡(W,𝐦)=s⁡(Wt,𝐦)s(W;\mathbf{m})=s(W_{t};\mathbf{m}). On the other hand, W0=Vν⁡(W)⊂ℂ⁡[x1,…,xn]W_{0}=V_{\nu(W)}\subset\mathbb{C}[x_{1},\ldots,x_{n}] since Fu=cu​u​xu+t⋅(higher term)F_{u}=c_{uu}x^{u}+t\cdot(\text{higher term}) for some cu​u≠0c_{uu}\not=0. From these inequalities, we have s⁡(W,𝐦)≥s⁡(Vν⁡(W),𝐦)s(W;\mathbf{m})\geq s(V_{\nu(W)};\mathbf{m}). ∎

Now we can show the main theorem easily.

Theorem 5.8 (=Theorem 1.3).

Let W∙W_{\bullet} be a birational graded linear series associated to a line bundle LL on an nn-dimensional variety XX. Fix a local coordinate system z=(z1,…,zn)z=(z_{1},\ldots,z_{n}) on XX at a smooth point and a monomial order >> on ℕn\mathbb{N}^{n}. Then ε⁡(W∙,𝐦)≥ε⁡(Δz,>​(W∙),𝐦)\varepsilon(W_{\bullet};\mathbf{m})\geq\varepsilon(\Delta_{z,>}(W_{\bullet});\mathbf{m}) holds for any r∈ℤ+r\in{\mathbb{Z}}_{+} and 𝐦∈ℝ+r\mathbf{m}\in{\mathbb{R}}_{+}^{r}.

Proof.

Let Γ:=ΓW∙,z,>⊂ℕ×ℕn\Gamma:=\Gamma_{W_{\bullet},z,>}\subset\mathbb{N}\times\mathbb{N}^{n} be the semigroup defined by W∙,zW_{\bullet},z, and >>. Then we have Γk=ν⁡(Wk)⊂ℕn\Gamma_{k}=\nu(W_{k})\subset\mathbb{N}^{n} and Δ⁡(Γ)=Δz,>​(W∙)\Delta(\Gamma)=\Delta_{z,>}(W_{\bullet}) by definition. By Proposition 5.7, it holds that

ε⁡(W∙,𝐦)=lims⁡(Wk,𝐦)k≥lims⁡(Vν⁡(Wk),𝐦)k=lims⁡(VΓk,𝐦)k.\varepsilon(W_{\bullet};\mathbf{m})=\lim\dfrac{s(W_{k};\mathbf{m})}{k}\geq\lim\dfrac{s(V_{\nu(W_{k})};\mathbf{m})}{k}=\lim\dfrac{s(V_{\Gamma_{k}};\mathbf{m})}{k}.

Since Γ\Gamma is birational by Lemma 5.3, we have

lims⁡(VΓk,𝐦)k=ε⁡(W​(Γ)∙,𝐦)=ε⁡(Δ⁡(Γ),𝐦)=ε⁡(Δz,>​(W∙),𝐦)\lim\dfrac{s(V_{\Gamma_{k}};\mathbf{m})}{k}=\varepsilon(W(\Gamma)_{\bullet};\mathbf{m})=\varepsilon(\Delta(\Gamma);\mathbf{m})=\varepsilon(\Delta_{z,>}(W_{\bullet});\mathbf{m})

from Lemma 5.6. Thus ε⁡(W∙,𝐦)≥ε⁡(Δz,>​(W∙),𝐦)\varepsilon(W_{\bullet};\mathbf{m})\geq\varepsilon(\Delta_{z,>}(W_{\bullet});\mathbf{m}) holds. ∎

Remark 5.9.

The inequality in Theorem 5.8 is not equality in general. Let LL be an ample line bundle on a projective variety XX. Let zz be a local coordinate system at pp and EE the prime divisor on XX defined by the first coordinate z1z_{1} of zz around pp. If >> is the lexicographic order, Δz,>​(L)\Delta_{z,>}(L) is contained in [0,a]×ℝdimX−1[0,a]\times\mathbb{R}^{\dim X-1}, where a=sup{t>0|L−t​E​ is effective}a=\sup\{\,t>0\,|\,L-tE\text{ is effective}\} (cf. [LM]). Hence ε⁡(Δz,>​(L),1)≤a\varepsilon(\Delta_{z,>}(L);1)\leq a holds (cf. [It, Theorem 3.6]). If we choose zz so that E∈|m​L|E\in|mL| for m≫0m\gg 0, we have ε⁡(Δz,>​(L),1)≤a=1/m<ε⁡(L,1)\varepsilon(\Delta_{z,>}(L);1)\leq a=1/m<\varepsilon(L;1).

Remark 5.10.

See [LM, Remark 5.5] for another relation between Okounkov bodies and Seshadri constants, though the relation is not written explicitly there. The relation also holds for a birational graded linear series.
